extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methods for proving and disproving mathematical statements (counterexamples, contradiction, induction, strong induction, smallest counterexample) aimed at students learning rigorous proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disprove P: Prove ∼P
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P, prove ∼P. In theory this proof can be carried out by direct, contrapositive or contradiction approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our approach is incredibly simple. To disprove P, prove ∼P. In practice choose a proof method (direct, contrapositive, contradiction) appropriate to the form of P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving a universal statement (counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to disprove ∀ x ∈ S, P(x). Produce an example of an x ∈ S that makes P(x) false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The negation ∼(∀ x ∈ S, P(x)) = ∃ x ∈ S, ∼P(x) is an existence statement — exhibit one x ∈ S with ∼P(x). Example: show n=11 makes f(n) composite to disprove 'f(n) is prime for all n'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving a conditional statement with a counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: How to disprove P(x) ⇒ Q(x). Produce an example of an x that makes P(x) true and Q(x) false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conditional fails exactly when there exists an x with P(x) true and Q(x) false. Explicitly display such an x and verify P(x) and ¬Q(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how the counterexample falsifies the statement
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting a counterexample, explain exactly how it makes the statement false rather than merely naming the counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., show the factorization f(11)=11·11 rather than just stating 'n=11'. Demonstrate the computation or reasoning that establishes ¬P(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving existence statements (prove universal negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove ∃ x ∈ S, P(x), prove its negation ∼(∃ x ∈ S, P(x)) = ∀ x ∈ S, ∼P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The negation is universally quantified, so an example does not suffice. Use direct proof, contrapositive, or contradiction to show ∼P(x) holds for every x ∈ S. Example: use contradiction to show no real x satisfies x^4 < x < x^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three major methods of proving statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The three major methods of proving a statement are direct proof, contrapositive proof and proof by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods can be applied both to proving statements and to proving negations when disproving statements; choose the method suited to the logical form of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disprove P with contradiction (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to disprove P with contradiction: Assume P is true, and deduce a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since ¬¬P = P, to prove ¬P by contradiction one typically assumes P and finds a logical contradiction; summarize the steps and conclude P is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by (simple) induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∀ n ∈ N, S_n by induction: (1) prove the basis step (S_1 or S_0 or stated base); (2) prove for any k ≥ base that S_k ⇒ S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize as dominoes: show first falls and each k forces k+1. Use direct proof for the inductive step by assuming S_k (the inductive hypothesis). Be careful which index is the base (S_0, S_1, or S_m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and base-case caveats for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The first statement in an induction may be S_1, S_0, or S_m depending on the problem; adjust the basis step accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proving ∀ n ∈ Z statements by induction, additional implications (Sk ⇒ Sk−1) or different bases may be required. The outline only proves for indices ≥ the chosen base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong induction: (1) prove initial base case(s); (2) assume S_1 ∧ S_2 ∧ ... ∧ S_k and prove this implies S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when S_k alone doesn't force S_{k+1} but several previous statements together do. Often requires verifying multiple initial cases so the 'window' of prior truths is available (e.g., S_1..S_6).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use strong induction (practical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong induction when assuming S_k alone does not yield S_{k+1}, but some earlier S_m (m<k) together imply S_{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving divisibility properties or tree-edge-count where removing an edge produces components of smaller sizes; check enough base cases so Sk−t ⇒ Sk+1 works for all k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by smallest counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: Smallest-counterexample method: (1) check the first statement; (2) assume not all S_n are true; (3) let k>1 be the smallest n with S_k false; (4) use that S_{k−1} is true and S_k false to derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hybrid of induction and contradiction is useful to obtain a direct contradiction from the coexistence of a minimal false case and its predecessors; commonly used for uniqueness or existence assertions (e.g., Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving existence vs. disproving existence (explicit vs universal)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an existence claim ∃ x P(x), give a concrete example; to disprove it, prove ∀ x ¬P(x) (see disproof of existence statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence proofs typically succeed by construction or example (e.g., x=2,y=16,z=4 for x^y = y^z). Disproofs require universal arguments and cannot rely on counterexamples.
